playable.title: The Day Before the Water
playable.record_caveat: This scenario compresses Katrina to one day, Sunday 28 August 2005 (Central Daylight Time): the day of the first-ever mandatory evacuation order, the Superdome's opening as a refuge of last resort, the National Weather Service's "devastating damage" statement and the end of contraflow. The clock stops on Sunday evening. Landfall came at 06:10 on Monday and the levee failures that flooded the city came on Monday morning, after the last decision on the desk, so the debrief shows them and the desk does not. "Impact" for scoring is therefore not the flood: it is the first documented onset of the storm on the Louisiana coast (NHC's 4 PM advisory: sustained tropical-storm-force winds, conditions to "worsen through the night"), after which NHC said preparations should be completed. "First public alert" is the City's first mandatory order; the City had called a voluntary evacuation on Saturday and parishes began evacuating from 09:00 Saturday, so the lead time shown measures the mandatory order only. The record disagrees about when that order came: the Senate committee's timeline says about 09:30, the House committee's report says around 11:00, and the National Weather Service assessment says 11 a.m.; this scenario uses 09:30. The CNN transcript of the joint news conference that the Senate cites is headed "Aired August 28, 2005 - 10:00 ET" (09:00 CDT), with the anchors still waiting for the Mayor to speak. The record also disagrees on the end of contraflow (about 17:00 in the Senate timeline, about 18:00 in the House report), and the two reports give different counts of the Superdome's pre-positioned rations, so no ration count is used. The player is cast as the City's top decision-maker, with the Governor's staff and the state emergency operations centre on the line. Some beats, such as the federal requests and contraflow, belonged to the Governor, the State Police and the state transportation department; they are framed as what the city could ask for. Some information shown, such as the 11:00 federal video teleconference and the Governor's Saturday request, is in the record but is not shown to have reached the Mayor, and the record does not say when the Mayor saw each item. Not read: the Louisiana state EOC conference-call audio, the New Orleans emergency plan itself (quoted through the House report), the Mayor's and Governor's own accounts beyond what the committees quote, and IPET volumes beyond Volume I. Where this scenario cannot say what a different decision would have caused, it says so: the record is silent on every path not taken.

info_available.text: NHC Special Advisory 22, 07:00: Katrina is "now a potentially catastrophic Category Five hurricane", maximum sustained winds near 160 mph, about 250 miles south-southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi. A Hurricane Warning is in effect from Morgan City, Louisiana, to the Alabama/Florida border, "including the city of New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain", and "preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion". Coastal storm surge flooding of 15 to 20 feet above normal tide, locally as high as 25 feet, is expected near and east of where the centre makes landfall.
info_available.headline: Katrina is "now a potentially catastrophic Category Five hurricane"

citation.detail: Special Advisory 22, 7 AM CDT Sun 28 Aug 2005

info_available.text: Saturday evening: at about 19:00 the National Weather Service advised the City of New Orleans Office of Emergency Preparedness that the New Orleans levees could be overtopped. From 19:25 to 20:00 NHC Director Max Mayfield briefed Governor Blanco, Governor Barbour and Mayor Nagin on Katrina's potential impact. At 22:00 NHC issued its first official storm-surge forecast, 15 to 20 feet above normal tides and locally as high as 25 feet.
info_available.headline: the New Orleans levees could be overtopped

citation.detail: Chapter 5, Timeline of Key Events, Saturday 27 August: 7 p.m. (NWS to the City OEP), 7:25-8 p.m. (Mayfield briefings), 10 p.m. (first storm-surge forecast)

info_available.text: Where the city stands. At about 13:00 on Saturday the Mayor declared a state of emergency at a joint news conference with the Governor and announced a voluntary evacuation; he asked residents of Algiers, the Lower Ninth Ward and low-lying areas to start leaving, and said the Superdome would open at 08:00 Sunday as a special-needs shelter. Contraflow, the highways running outbound only, began at about 16:00 on Saturday.
info_available.headline: the Mayor declared a state of emergency

citation.detail: Chapter 5 timeline, Saturday 27 August: ~1 p.m. and 4 p.m.; Chapter 16 (Pre-Storm Evacuations) (Mayor's Saturday press conference)

info_available.text: The mandatory evacuation order is still being drafted. The Mayor told staff at noon on Saturday to begin it. A draft sent round late Saturday night excepts essential personnel of the city, regulated utilities, hospitals and their patients, and operating hotels and their guests; staff have since added the media and nursing-home personnel, and Colonel Terry Ebbert, Director of Homeland Security and Public Safety, has recommended that nursing homes not be excepted. Still open: who is excepted, how the order would be enforced, and what transport the city has.
info_available.headline: The mandatory evacuation order is still being drafted.

citation.detail: Chapter 16 (Pre-Storm Evacuations), "Mayor Nagin issued a mandatory-evacuation order ... on Sunday" and notes 60-64

info_available.text: The city's own emergency plan lets the Mayor "direct and compel, by any necessary and reasonable force, the evacuation of all or part of the population from any stricken or threatened area within the City if he deems this action necessary for the preservation of life". The same plan acknowledges that "[a]pproximately 100,000 Citizens of New Orleans do not have means of personal transportation".
info_available.headline: 100,000 Citizens of New Orleans do not have means of personal transportation

citation.detail: Chapter "Evacuation": quotations of the New Orleans plan under "The declarations of a 'mandatory' evacuation were delayed ..." and "The shelter of last resort ... was inadequate"

options.label: Issue the mandatory evacuation order now, on the draft as it stands
options.detail: Order Orleans Parish to evacuate this hour with the exceptions as drafted, announce it on every channel, and settle enforcement and transport in the hours that follow.

options.label: Hold the order until its exceptions, enforcement and transport questions are settled
options.detail: The draft is nearly there. Finish the exceptions list, the enforcement plan and the transport question first, then announce.

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. The Mayor had told staff at noon on Saturday to begin the order; it was announced on Sunday morning, at about 09:30 by the Senate committee's timeline and about 11:00 by the House committee's. The Senate found the city "took nearly 24 hours" to resolve legal and logistical questions, and that the Mayor "wasted time in waiting to order a mandatory evacuation until Sunday morning, while his staff worked out details of the order that should have been settled long before the crisis".

citation.detail: Chapter 16 (Pre-Storm Evacuations); Finding 60; Chapter 5 timeline, Sunday 28 August, 9:30 a.m.

options.label: Stay with the voluntary evacuation and press it harder
options.detail: Keep the Saturday call and add door-knocking by police and fire, church networks, and a second round of TV and radio messages to the low-lying neighbourhoods.

historical_citation.detail: Chapter 16 (Pre-Storm Evacuations) (order ordered drafted at noon Saturday; issued Sunday morning); Finding 60

info_available.text: About 09:30 the city issues its first-ever mandatory evacuation order, at a joint news conference with the Governor. "I wish I had better news for you," the Mayor says. "But we are facing a storm that most of us have feared." The final order excepts essential personnel of federal, state and city government, regulated utilities and mass transit, hospitals and their patients, the media, the Orleans Parish Criminal Sheriff's Office and its inmates, and operating hotels and their patrons. "We sent out a fax to all the churches that we could this morning," he says, asking them to "buddy up" and check on seniors who rely on public transport.
info_available.headline: About 09:30 the city issues its first-ever mandatory evacuation order

citation.detail: Chapter 16 (Pre-Storm Evacuations), text and note 57 (Mayor's statement; final exceptions list); Chapter 5 timeline, 9:30 a.m.

info_available.text: At the same news conference the Governor says President Bush telephoned her just before and "asked me to please ensure that there would be a mandatory evacuation of New Orleans". She says waters could be as high as 15 to 20 feet, which is what the National Hurricane Center "has shared with us". The Mayor says: "The storm surge most likely will topple our levee system."
info_available.headline: "The storm surge most likely will topple our levee system."

citation.detail: Chapter "Evacuation": Nagin-Blanco news conference, 28 August 2005, as quoted under "The declarations of a 'mandatory' evacuation were delayed or never made"

info_available.text: The Mayor announces that the Superdome will open to the general public at 12:00 as a refuge of last resort, and names 12 pick-up points where Regional Transit Authority buses will collect people for it, among them the E.J. Morris Senior Center, Frantz in the Ninth Ward, Warren Easton and Augustine in Mid-City and O. Perry Walker High School on the West Bank. The city waited until Saturday to announce the Superdome, fearing that saying so earlier might dissuade people from leaving.
info_available.headline: the Superdome will open to the general public at 12:00 as a refuge of last resort

citation.detail: Chapter 16, note 57 (Superdome at 12 p.m.; 12 RTA pick-up points); Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "The City Prepares and Opens the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort"

info_available.text: The Regional Transit Authority owns 372 buses and employs 650 drivers; it estimates each bus can take 40 people and their luggage out of the city, and about 100 drivers have volunteered for evacuation duty. The RTA has offered its buses and drivers; the director of the city's Office of Emergency Preparedness, Chief Matthews, has turned down the offers, citing a lack of identifiable shelters.
info_available.headline: Chief Matthews, has turned down the offers, citing a lack of identifiable shelters

citation.detail: Chapter 16, "The Director of the City of New Orleans Office of Emergency Preparedness Turned Down Offers of Assistance ... From the Regional Transit Authority"

options.label: Take up the RTA's offer: run its buses out of the city, and ask the state for more drivers
options.detail: Send the RTA buses from the pick-up points to shelters beyond the flood, not just to the Superdome, and ask the Governor's staff for drivers, buses and a destination outside the city.

options.label: Open the Superdome at noon as the refuge of last resort and run RTA buses to it from the 12 pick-up points
options.detail: Have police and fire go through the city asking people to go to the pick-up points; buses take them to the Superdome, where the National Guard screens them in.

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. After the order, city officials sent police and fire through the city "asking" people to go to checkpoints where buses would take them, but only as far as the Superdome, opened at noon as a refuge of last resort; bus service began at noon. The House committee wrote that "the city did not make arrangements for their evacuation" and instead "decided to shelter them in New Orleans".

citation.detail: Chapter "Evacuation": "The shelter of last resort for those who could not or would not evacuate was inadequate"; Senate Chapter 11 gives the noon start of bus service

options.label: Announce the order and leave the rest to contraflow, churches and neighbours
options.detail: No city buses. Rely on the highways, the church buddy system started this morning and residents' own cars to move people.

historical_citation.detail: Chapter "Evacuation", "The shelter of last resort for those who could not or would not evacuate was inadequate"

info_available.text: NWS New Orleans/Baton Rouge, 10:11, an urgent message headed "...DEVASTATING DAMAGE EXPECTED...": Katrina is "A MOST POWERFUL HURRICANE WITH UNPRECEDENTED STRENGTH...RIVALING THE INTENSITY OF HURRICANE CAMILLE OF 1969." "MOST OF THE AREA WILL BE UNINHABITABLE FOR WEEKS...PERHAPS LONGER." "WATER SHORTAGES WILL MAKE HUMAN SUFFERING INCREDIBLE BY MODERN STANDARDS." For Orleans and neighbouring parishes the inland hurricane wind warning says tropical-storm-force winds will begin around 3 PM, and hurricane-force winds around sunset in Lower Plaquemines, spreading north by 3 AM Monday: "DO NOT VENTURE OUTSIDE!"
info_available.headline: "MOST OF THE AREA WILL BE UNINHABITABLE FOR WEEKS...PERHAPS LONGER."

info_available.text: NHC Advisory 23, 10:00: Katrina is "even stronger", maximum sustained winds near 175 mph, pressure 907 mb; hurricane-force winds extend 105 miles from the centre, tropical-storm-force winds 205 miles. The storm surge forecast is raised to 18 to 22 feet above normal tide, locally as high as 28 feet, "along with large and dangerous battering waves". The Hurricane Warning stays up for New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain.
info_available.headline: The storm surge forecast is raised to 18 to 22 feet above normal tide

citation.detail: Advisory 23, 10 AM CDT Sun 28 Aug 2005

info_available.text: At 11:00 the daily federal video teleconference, linking the White House, DHS, FEMA and its regional offices with Louisiana and Mississippi, takes place. NHC's Max Mayfield: "I don't think any model can tell you with any confidence right now whether the levees will be topped or not, but that's obviously a very, very grave concern." FEMA Director Michael Brown: "Just keep jamming those lines full as much as you can with commodities." On this call and Saturday's, state officials report that contraflow is going well.
info_available.headline: whether the levees will be topped or not, but that's obviously a very, very grave concern.

citation.detail: Chapter 5 timeline, Sunday 28 August, 11 a.m. (note 31); Chapter 16, "Governor Blanco Did Not Request Transportation Resources From the Federal Government"

info_available.text: On Saturday the Governor asked the President for $9 million in Stafford Act assistance for emergency protective measures, of which $2.5 million was for evacuation needs; the request did not specify a need for transportation. The President granted the emergency declaration the same day.
info_available.headline: the request did not specify a need for transportation

citation.detail: Chapter 16, "Governor Blanco Did Not Request Transportation Resources From the Federal Government"

options.label: Ask FEMA and the Department of Transportation for buses and drivers to take people out of New Orleans before the storm
options.detail: Use the call, and the Governor's line to the White House, to put a specific request for evacuation buses and drivers on the record while the roads are still open.

options.label: Ask for military and Coast Guard boats, helicopters and medical teams to be staged within range for the morning after
options.detail: Request pre-positioned rescue and medical assets, in addition to commodities, so that they can fly or float in the hour the winds drop.

options.label: Report that contraflow is working and welcome the federal commodities; make no request for transport
options.detail: Contraflow has moved the people who had cars. Thank FEMA for the supplies on their way and move on.

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. State officials discussed the success of contraflow on the Saturday and Sunday calls but did not raise additional transportation assets, despite the long-standing knowledge that 100,000 people in New Orleans lacked transportation; neither the Governor nor any other state official made a specific request of the federal government for transportation resources before landfall. The Senate found the Governor "missed opportunities to ask the federal government to help evacuate New Orleans before landfall".

citation.detail: Chapter 16, "Governor Blanco Did Not Request Transportation Resources From the Federal Government"; Finding 62

historical_citation.detail: Chapter 16, "Governor Blanco Did Not Request Transportation Resources From the Federal Government"; Findings 62, 65 and 66

info_available.text: The Superdome opens to the general public at 12:00 as the refuge of last resort, and RTA bus service from the pick-up points begins. The special-needs shelter inside has been open since 08:00; it was set up for about 1,200 people, 600 special-needs patients and their caregivers. In earlier hurricanes the Superdome served as a refuge for those riding out a storm for a few hours before going home. Since Hurricane Ivan in 2004 the city's plan has been to use RTA buses to bring people without transportation to it.
info_available.headline: The Superdome opens to the general public at 12:00 as the refuge of last resort

citation.detail: Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "Preparing the Superdome as a Special-Needs Shelter" and "Preparing the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort"; Chapter 5 timeline, Sunday 28 August, 8 a.m. and 12 p.m.

info_available.text: This morning city officials were drafting a plan to seize private facilities to create additional refuges of last resort. The city's Director of Homeland Security, Terry Ebbert, predicts "nightmare" conditions in the Superdome.
info_available.headline: predicts "nightmare" conditions in the Superdome

citation.detail: Chapter "Evacuation": "The shelter of last resort for those who could not or would not evacuate was inadequate"

info_available.text: As of Sunday no one has made arrangements for portable toilets at the Superdome: on Saturday the city Health Director, Dr. Kevin Stephens, tried to contract with individual vendors but could not reach them. National Guard and FEMA food and water have been pre-positioned there.
info_available.headline: As of Sunday no one has made arrangements for portable toilets at the Superdome

citation.detail: Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "The City Prepares and Opens the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort"; House, "Those in shelters or on high ground suffered horrible conditions" (pre-positioned food and water)

options.label: Open the Superdome now, and in the same hour order toilets, water, food, medical staff and police in bulk from the state and FEMA
options.detail: Put the whole supply list to the state EOC and FEMA before the first bus arrives, rather than adding to it as the crowd grows.

options.label: Open the Superdome with what is on site and add supplies as the crowd shows up
options.detail: Doors at noon, National Guard and police screening at the door, the pre-positioned stock in hand; ask for more as numbers become clear.

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. By late Sunday evening about 10,000 people had shown up. Officials realised during Sunday that more supplies were needed and rushed out requests, including for 350,000 more meals-ready-to-eat from the city and more food and water from the state; no one had arranged portable toilets; and a FEMA medical team, which the city accepted help from on Sunday, stopped in Baton Rouge when the Texas State Police denied two requests for escorts and did not reach the Superdome before landfall.

citation.detail: Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "Sheltering in the Superdome" and "The City Prepares and Opens the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort"

options.label: Open a second refuge of last resort now, using the plan drafted this morning, and split the bus runs
options.detail: Designate a second large building on the plan to commandeer private facilities, so the Superdome is not the only place the buses go.

historical_citation.detail: Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "Preparing the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort"; House, Chapter "Evacuation", "The shelter of last resort ... was inadequate" ("Only at the last minute did the City ask for food and water and medical personnel")

info_available.text: NHC Advisory 24, 16:00: Katrina is a Category Five hurricane, maximum sustained winds near 165 mph, pressure 902 mb, about 150 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi. "Sustained tropical storm force winds are occurring over the southeast Louisiana coast": Southwest Pass reports sustained winds of 48 mph with gusts to 53. "Conditions are already beginning to deteriorate ... and will continue to worsen through the night." Surge of 18 to 22 feet, locally 28, with large and dangerous battering waves: "Some levees in the greater New Orleans area could be overtopped." "Preparations to protect life and property should be completed this evening."
info_available.headline: "Some levees in the greater New Orleans area could be overtopped."

citation.detail: Advisory 24, 4 PM CDT Sun 28 Aug 2005

info_available.text: Contraflow, all highway lanes outbound, has run since about 16:00 on Saturday, managed by the state transportation department and the State Police, with the Governor monitoring it personally. Louisiana's plan, coordinated with Mississippi and Texas, had the southernmost parishes leave first so that evacuees would not meet bottlenecks in New Orleans or Baton Rouge. RTA special service runs from 12 sites to the Superdome, and at least 10 paratransit vehicles are carrying special-needs residents to the Baton Rouge area.
info_available.headline: Contraflow, all highway lanes outbound, has run since about 16:00 on Saturday

citation.detail: Chapter "Pre-landfall Preparation and Katrina's Impact", "Evacuations in Louisiana" (contraflow; RTA special service)

options.label: Keep contraflow running through the evening, until the outbound lanes are empty or the weather closes the road
options.detail: Ask the State Police to hold the lanes outbound for latecomers, carpoolers and anyone the church network has found a ride for.

options.label: Let the State Police end contraflow this evening, once traffic is light
options.detail: Traffic is thinning; return the lanes to their normal configuration, with the outbound lanes still open to anyone leaving.

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. By 6:00 p.m. on Sunday traffic was light, so contraflow was halted; residents could still leave on the outbound lanes once the highways were returned to their normal configuration. The Senate committee's timeline places the end of contraflow at 5 p.m.

citation.detail: Chapter "Pre-landfall Preparation and Katrina's Impact", "Evacuations in Louisiana": "By 6:00 p.m. on Sunday, August 28, traffic was light, so contraflow was halted"; Senate Chapter 5 timeline, 5 p.m.

options.label: Keep the outbound lanes for the city's buses and vans, carrying people to Baton Rouge and beyond
options.detail: Reserve the contraflow lanes for RTA buses and paratransit vans on runs out of the city, as long as drivers will make them.

historical_citation.detail: Chapter "Pre-landfall Preparation and Katrina's Impact", "Evacuations in Louisiana": contraflow ran from Saturday about 4:00 p.m. and was halted on Sunday when traffic was light

MAXIMUM WIND GUSTS AROUND 175 MPH ARE LIKELY IN THE WARNED AREA BY DAYBREAK MONDAY." "DO NOT VENTURE OUTDOORS ONCE TROPICAL STORM FORCE WINDS ONSET."

info_available.text: NHC Intermediate Advisory 24A, 19:00: about 130 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi, winds near 160 mph, pressure 904 mb, moving north-northwest at 11 mph. "Sustained tropical storm force winds are already occurring over the southeast Louisiana coast." "Some levees in the greater New Orleans area could be overtopped." "Winds affecting the upper floors of high-rise buildings will be significantly stronger than those near ground level." Preparations "should be completed this evening".
info_available.headline: tropical storm force winds are already occurring over the southeast Louisiana coast

citation.detail: Intermediate Advisory 24A, 7 PM CDT Sun 28 Aug 2005

info_available.text: The downpour began at the Superdome around 18:00 and security screening moved inside the building, which made it harder for city police to ensure that no one entered with a weapon. Contraflow has been halted: traffic was light by about 18:00. Under the contraflow plan the roads are closed a few hours before landfall.
info_available.headline: Contraflow has been halted: traffic was light by about 18:00.

citation.detail: Chapter 11 ("The New Orleans Scenario"), "The City Prepares and Opens the Superdome as a Refuge of Last Resort" (security, 6 p.m. downpour); Chapter 16, RTA drivers (roads closed "a few hours before landfall", consistent with the contraflow plan)

options.label: Keep the buses running to the Superdome into the night, for as long as drivers will go
options.detail: Hold the pick-up points open and the shuttles moving in the rain, using the volunteer drivers, and accept the weather risk.

options.label: Stand the buses down at about 19:00 as conditions worsen

consequence.text: This is the path the day took. All RTA bus service ceased at approximately 7:00 p.m. on Sunday, about 11 hours before Katrina was due to make landfall and as conditions worsened. More than 70,000 people remained in the city to be rescued after the storm.

playable.title: The Day the Fire Came Back
playable.location: Lahaina and Upcountry, Maui, Hawaiʻi, USA
playable.record_caveat: The record here is strong on times and thin on reasons. The minute-by-minute facts come from the FSRI timeline dataset published for the Hawaiʻi Attorney General (dispatch audio, police and fire logs, MEMA and HI-EMA logs, NWS products, Hawaiian Electric statements, county social-media posts, and the administrator's own text messages), and from FSRI's Phase Two analysis of 13 September 2024. The Phase One report PDF could not be read as text, so Phase One facts are cited to its dataset rows by time and source. The county after-action report by the Western Fire Chiefs Association and MPD's own report could not be retrieved, and are not cited. Some entries in the dataset carry wrong or later timestamps; those were left out. The player is cast as the MEMA Administrator, who the record places in Honolulu for the Pacific Partnership 2023 meeting that day; the EOC was run in Maui by his staff, and some information shown here (dispatch traffic, 911 calls) is in the county's records but is not shown to have reached him. FSRI's staff interviews say siren activation was not discussed on 8 August, while the Administrator said on 16 August he had decided against it; the documents available here do not reconcile the two. Where this scenario cannot say what a different decision would have caused, it says so: the record is silent on every path not taken. How much Hurricane Dora itself contributed to the wind has been questioned in later analyses; this scenario reports only what the forecasts said. The origin and cause of the fire are under separate investigation and are not addressed.

inquiry_findings.quote: Actionable extreme weather forecasts were provided to fire chiefs and emergency managers prior to the August 2023 fires. However, adjusting staffing for extreme weather events and their resultant risk of extreme fire behavior was not standard.

citation.detail: Finding 5, Appendix 6.1 (Section 3.2 Weather)

inquiry_findings.quote: Given the known conditions forecasted for the County of Maui on August 8, 2023, agency representatives self-reported to the EOC throughout the day, but full activation of the EOC did not occur until 16:30.

citation.detail: Finding 49, Appendix 6.1 (Section 3.6.4)

inquiry_findings.quote: Only one (1) siren from the All-Hazard Outdoor Warning Siren System was operable within the burn perimeter of the Lahaina area on August 8, 2023.
inquiry_findings.translation: Finding 37. The report's body text names two sirens listed as operable, MA407 and MA412, and says both were 'very likely inoperable' on 8 August because the area had intermittent cell service. It also says the County of Maui 'provided no evidence of discussing siren activation' on the day, and calls the effect of sirens 'an open question'.

citation.detail: Finding 37 (Appendix 6.1) and Section 3.5.1.2

inquiry_findings.quote: The effectiveness of warning sirens remains an open question.
inquiry_findings.translation: FSRI judged it unlikely that residents would have known what a siren signal meant that day, and also that activation 'may have provided an additional cue to alert residents of an emergency and to seek further information'.

citation.detail: Section 3.5.1.2, Outdoor Warning Siren System

inquiry_findings.quote: We were afraid that people would have gone mauka.
inquiry_findings.translation: Not an inquiry finding. The MEMA Administrator, 16 August 2023, explaining why sirens were not sounded; 'mauka' means toward the mountain. AP also quotes him: 'If that was the case, then they would have gone into the fire.' He resigned on 17 August, citing health reasons.

citation.detail: AP, 'Maui's emergency services chief resigns after facing criticism for not activating sirens during fire', 17 Aug 2023

takeaways.text: A forecast is not a plan: the extreme-weather warning reached fire chiefs and emergency managers ahead of the day, but turning it into extra staff was not standard practice.

citation.detail: Finding 5, Appendix 6.1 (Section 3.2 Weather)

takeaways.text: Activation is a decision, not a drift: with the conditions forecast, agencies reported to the EOC on their own through the day, and full activation came only at 16:30.

citation.detail: Finding 49, Appendix 6.1 (Section 3.6.4)

takeaways.text: Silence is a decision too: the County 'provided no evidence of discussing siren activation' that day — an open question about what sirens would have done is no reason never to ask it.

citation.detail: Finding 37 (Appendix 6.1) and Section 3.5.1.2

playable.title: The Million-Person Evacuation
playable.record_caveat: This is the success case, and its record is thinner than the US and Spanish inquiries. There is no public inquiry. The sources are IMD's own report on the storm (primary: bulletin times, forecasts, radar, tolls as supplied by the state), the joint Government of Odisha / World Bank / Asian Development Bank damage assessment, a slide presentation by an OSDMA chief general manager (undated), and three press reports. The Odisha government's own order-by-order timeline was not fetchable, so the record does not say at what hour any evacuation order was given, and most of the evacuation (the 36 hours before landfall) began on 11 October, before this clock opens. The clock is a single day because the game cannot cross midnight. Where an item comes from an undated source it is placed by plausibility and says so in its text. The IMD report stamps its warning bulletins in a day-hour-minute form with an unexplained suffix (for example 120630ef); they are read here as IST. The landfall hour varies inside IMD's own report (about 21:30 IST in its satellite section, 22:30 in its summary; radar shows the eye over land by 22:05) and in press (about 21:15). Wind figures are not comparable across agencies: IMD reports 3-minute winds, the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center 1-minute winds. Where this scenario cannot say what a different decision would have caused, it says so: the record is silent on every path not taken. The score is game design, not a claim about lives saved. The scoring field for the first public alert is set to the first listed bulletin of this day, 06:30, only because the clock cannot hold the real first alerts of 8 to 10 October.

deaths.note: Counts differ by what they include. 21 were killed by the cyclone itself (IMD's report, as supplied by the state; OSDMA). The floods that followed add 17 in IMD's report and 23 in OSDMA's table, and the joint damage assessment gives 44 dead in all. IMD lists one further death in coastal Andhra Pradesh. Press counts were 25 on 14 October (AP) and 21 on 16 October (Reuters). For comparison, the 1999 super cyclone is given as 'about 10,000' dead in the damage assessment, as 8,900 in OSDMA's comparison table, and as 8,243 in a government report quoted by Al Jazeera; this scenario does not resolve those to one figure. Evacuation is graded the same way: the state's own tally is 983,642 for the cyclone (and 171,083 more for the floods that followed), the damage assessment says 'over 1 million' within 36 hours, and the 1.2 million sometimes quoted rests on secondary summaries only.

playable.record_caveat: The record here is a judicial instruction still in progress, not a closed inquiry. Times and gauge figures come from official AEMET warnings, CHJ notifications entered in the Catarroja court file, and press reconstructions of that file; quotes from the investigating judge come from interlocutory orders as reproduced in press coverage, and are provisional. Where this scenario cannot say what a different decision would have caused, it says so: the record is silent on every path not taken.
